summary: Sets out IETF policies on intellectual property rights such as patents in IETF technology, so working groups know about any IPR constraints on a proposal. It was replaced by RFC 8179.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the group picks an idea, it wants to know if anyone owns a legal claim on it. This memo sets up how to tell. A newer rulebook replaced it.

questions: who must disclose patents in the ietf
subtitle: The 2005 rules requiring IETF participants to disclose patents and other IPR that cover technology under discussion.

tldr.problem: Working groups increasingly faced patent claims on technology they were discussing, and the intent of Section 10 of RFC 2026 on IPR disclosure was repeatedly debated.
tldr.mechanism: Anyone who reasonably and personally knows of IPR they believe covers or may cover a Contribution must disclose it in a timely way, the IETF takes no position on validity, and working groups weigh the disclosed licensing terms when choosing technology.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3979 was replaced by RFC 8179 and was also updated by RFC 4879, so it is no longer the current statement of the policy.

today: RFC 3979 is no longer current: it was obsoleted by RFC 8179 and was also updated by RFC 4879. It had replaced RFC 3668 and, with RFC 3978, replaced Section 10 of RFC 2026.

sections.title: Purpose and Principles
sections.content:
It is increasingly common for IETF working groups to deal with claims of intellectual property rights (IPR), such as patents, on technology under discussion. This memo (BCP 79) clarifies the IPR part of Section 10 of RFC 2026, without intending to change the policy. It is not legal advice, and a companion document, RFC 3978, covers copyrights and trademarks in Contributions.

Disclosures can come at any time: before the first draft, before publication, or after an RFC is out and the working group has closed. They may rest on granted patents or applications, and may even be made disingenuously to affect the process.

Three principles come from RFC 2026. The IETF makes no determination about the validity of any IPR claim. The IETF may decide to use technology that has disclosures if it finds the use warranted. And everyone contributing to a working group's discussions must disclose IPR they believe covers or may ultimately cover the technology. No patent search is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The group does not decide who is right about ownership. It only asks everyone to speak up about claims they know of, so choices are made with full information.

sections.title: Who Must Disclose, and When
sections.content:
A Contributor who reasonably and personally knows of IPR covering their own Contribution, or which their employer or sponsor may assert against implementations based on it, must make a disclosure; there are no exceptions. Any other participant who reasonably and personally knows of such IPR in someone else's Contribution must also disclose. People who know of IPR they are not required to disclose, for example IPR owned by another company, are encouraged to email ietf-ipr@ietf.org. An employer or owner disclosing in the person's place satisfies the duty.

The term reasonably and personally known means what the individual knows or would be expected to know from their job. An organization cannot keep a person in the dark to avoid disclosure, but no patent search is needed.

Disclosure must be made as soon as reasonably possible after the Contribution is published in an Internet-Draft, or after the person first learns of the IPR, unless an applicable disclosure is already on file. Preliminary disclosure is strongly encouraged earlier, once a contribution is seriously being discussed.

A disclosure must list issued patent numbers or published applications (or say the claim rests on unpublished applications) and the specific documents affected, with a version number for an Internet-Draft. A blanket statement of possible IPR on every Contribution does not satisfy the rule, and nor does a blanket promise to license on fair and non-discriminatory terms. A blanket promise to license royalty-free, with any other terms disclosed, does. Licensing detail is encouraged but not mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: If you know about a claim that touches an idea the group is discussing, you must say so soon, and say exactly what it touches. A vague note that you might own something does not count.

sections.title: What Happens After a Disclosure
sections.content:
When IPR is disclosed before publication, the RFC Editor ensures the resulting RFC notes that such claims exist. The IESG disclaims responsibility for finding or evaluating IPR and takes no position on validity or scope. The IETF Executive Director asks the discloser for a written assurance that, once the specification is approved, all persons can obtain the right to implement it under one of the licensing options in Section 6.5. The result does not by itself block publication or advancement, but the working group may weigh it and the IESG may defer approval to help obtain assurances. Results are recorded and made available online.

The IESG makes no explicit finding that reasonable and non-discriminatory terms were met. Instead it applies the normal advancement rules: it presumes the terms are reasonable and to some degree non-discriminatory if two unrelated implementations by different parties exist for Draft Standard, or the required operational experience exists for Standard. Anyone may challenge the presumption by emailing the IESG.

Every IETF RFC must carry a standard disclaimer of validity, saying the IETF takes no position on the validity or scope of any IPR and inviting anyone to report rights that may cover the technology. The documents themselves must not mention specific IPR, because readers could think the IETF has formed an opinion or that the list is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The group writes down the claims and asks the claimant for a promise to share fairly, but it does not rule on who is right. Every finished paper carries a note saying so.

sections.title: Weighing Technologies and Change Control
sections.content:
Working groups prefer technology with no known IPR claims or with an offer of royalty-free licensing, but have discretion to adopt technology with a fair and non-discriminatory commitment, or even none, if it is superior enough. An IETF consensus says a mandatory-to-implement security technology should not be specified unless it has no known IPR claims or a royalty-free license is available, absent a very good reason.

Having no disclosures does not mean none will come later, and a disclosure does not prove the IPR is valid or enforceable. Working groups may form their own opinions on this.

The IETF must have change control over technology in standards-track documents so it can fix problems. A developer may hand change control to the IETF, which can be complex; RFC 1790 and RFC 2339 are given as examples. A standards-track document may still refer normatively to proprietary technology.
sections.plainLanguage: The group likes ideas that anyone may use for free, but it can pick another if it is much better. It also wants the final say on changing any idea it publishes as a standard.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo relates to IETF process, not any particular technology. A working group should consider security as one part of evaluating a technology, just as IPR is one part, but there are no known issues of security with IPR procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: These are paperwork rules, so the memo says they do not cause new safety problems. Safety is something the group checks separately for each idea.
